summary: This document gives a problem statement and terminology for emergency callers who are not authenticated, have no identifiable service provider, or have no credit to pay for network access. It describes an extension to the IETF emergency services architecture.

eli5.summary: Anyone should be able to call for help even if they have no account. This RFC explains how emergency calls can still work in those cases.

subtitle: How emergency callers without accounts or service can still reach 911

tldr.problem: Internet emergency services require network authentication or a service provider account, but in emergencies, a caller might lack valid credentials, have no service account, or have no prepaid balance.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC extends the IETF emergency services architecture to handle three special cases: No Access Authentication (NAA), No ASP (service provider), and Zero-balance ASP, allowing emergency calls through alternative paths when normal authentication fails.
tldr.outcome: Networks can support emergency calls even from unauthenticated or unauthorized users, matching PSTN expectations, though this requires careful security measures to prevent abuse and hoax calls.

today: RFC 7406 is an Informational RFC that extends the IETF emergency services architecture defined in RFC 6881 and RFC 6443. It provides guidance but does not mandate implementation of any of the three cases; deployment depends on local regulation and ISP policy.

sections.title: Emergency Calls Without Normal Access
sections.content:
The IETF emergency services architecture divides responsibility among three parties: the access network (Internet Service Provider), the application service provider (VoIP service), and the emergency service network (the 911 system). In normal operation, callers are authenticated by one or both.

But emergencies are different. A person stranded without a phone, a visitor with a device but no local service account, or a caller with an expired prepaid account should still be able to reach emergency services. This RFC addresses three distinct cases where a caller cannot follow the normal authentication flow but needs emergency help.
sections.eli5: In normal times, only authorized people can use a network. But in emergencies, anyone nearby should be able to call for help, even without an account.

sections.title: Three Special Cases
sections.content:
No Access Authentication (NAA): The device has no valid credentials for the access network (ISP). This includes pay-per-use wireless hotspots where there is insufficient time to enter credit card information. The ISP must decide whether to allow emergency calls under this circumstance.

No ASP (NASP): The caller has network access but has no VoIP service account or all reachable accounts are not available. The caller can reach the network but cannot use any service provider to make calls. This case is common with visitors or people between service changes.

Zero-balance ASP (ZBP): The caller is known to a service provider and can be authenticated, but is not authorized to use services (prepaid account depleted, contract expired, account restricted). The service provider can verify identity but might refuse authorization for regular calls.
sections.eli5: There are three problems: no account with the internet provider, no account with the phone company, or a phone company account with no money left. Each needs a different solution.

sections.title: Network Attachment for Emergency Callers
sections.content:
When an emergency caller initiates a call without normal credentials, the network must first grant some form of access. For NAA cases, the link layer (Ethernet, WiFi, cellular) must support an emergency access mode, possibly indicated through Layer 2 signaling or special network names. This is technology-specific and not standardized in the RFC.

Once the device obtains basic link-layer access, it uses DHCP to get an IP configuration from the ISP. It then performs location determination through standard location protocols, and uses the Location-to-Service Translation (LoST) protocol to discover which emergency service provider (ESRP) to contact for its geographic location. Finally, the SIP User Agent initiates an emergency SIP INVITE containing location information.
sections.eli5: First, the device gets permission to talk to the network with a special 'emergency only' mode. Then it learns its location and finds out who the local emergency services are.

sections.title: Service Provider and Emergency Service Handling
sections.content:
For NASP cases, the emergency caller's SIP UA contacts the ESRP (Emergency Service Routing Proxy) directly, bypassing the service provider's normal proxy. This requires that the end device, not a service provider, generate the SIP INVITE. The ESRP must be able to process emergency calls from unknown sources.

For ZBP cases, an authenticated caller with the service provider can attempt emergency call authorization separately from regular service authorization. A service provider may allow emergency calls even when regular services are barred, but this is a policy decision. If denied, the caller can fall back to NASP procedures.

All cases require the end device to discover location information and to perform LoST lookup to find the correct emergency service destination. The emergency service network must understand Service URN markers (urn:service:sos) that identify emergency calls.
sections.eli5: Either the device calls emergency services directly or asks the phone company to let emergency calls through even if the account is blocked.

sections.title: Security and Fraud Prevention
sections.content:
Allowing emergency calls without authentication creates new security and fraud concerns. When the Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP) has no identity information about the caller, hoax and test calls become a significant problem.

Real-world experience from cellular networks shows that SIM-less emergency calling in some countries led to high volumes of false calls that overloaded emergency services. To mitigate abuse, ISPs can restrict unauthenticated emergency traffic to only the LoST server and the discovered PSAP URI, using traffic filtering. Service providers can verify that emergency calls go only to legitimate emergency numbers returned by LoST.

The RFC emphasizes that these mitigations are architectural choices and implementation-specific; detailed filtering methods depend on the ISP's network design and are not standardized.
sections.eli5: Allowing calls without real names risks fake emergency calls clogging the system. Networks have to set up rules to stop people from making hoax calls.

sections.title: Extending the Architecture
sections.content:
RFC 7406 extends the baseline emergency services architecture by defining how three distinct cases—NAA, NASP, and ZBP—are handled when normal authentication fails. Each case requires different support from different network entities.

NAA support is a Layer 2 (link layer) decision and is technology-specific. NASP requires that end devices and emergency service proxies support the full emergency call flow without a service provider. ZBP requires service providers to make policy decisions about which callers can place emergency calls despite authorization failures. All cases depend on location determination, LoST discovery, and SIP emergency call handling already specified in related RFCs.
sections.eli5: This document explains how three different types of emergency callers—those without network access, without a phone account, or without account credit—can get help by using existing emergency call systems in special ways.
